blockers.quote: 632 people kept a diary of their lies for 91 days (c15).
blockers.why: Row c15 verbatim quote ('Across participants, lying comprised 7% of total communication and almost 90% of all lies were little white lies.') contains neither the participant count '632' nor '91 days', nor does it support that participants 'kept a diary' (c15 was a communication tracking study, while diary studies were c01 and c11). Stating spoken digits 632 and 91 and claiming a diary format exceeds what the row's verbatim quote supports.
blockers.fix: In another large study, most people lied rarely. A few prolific liars told most of the lies (c17).

blockers.quote: In developmental studies, most children aged 3 to 8 who were told not to peek at a toy peeked, then lied about it (c16).
blockers.why: Scope overstatement. Row c16 covers a single study (Talwar & Lee 2008: 'Children (3-8 years) were told not to peek at a toy. Most children peeked and later lied about peeking.'). Generalizing the single experiment cited in c16 to 'In developmental studies' plural overstates the scope beyond what the source supports.
blockers.fix: In one study, most children aged 3 to 8 who were told not to peek at a toy peeked, then lied about it (c16).

blockers.quote: In a US national survey of 1,000 adults, about 60% reported no lies at all in the past day (c03).
blockers.why: Row c03 verbatim quote ('Sixty percent of subjects report telling no lies at all, and almost half of all lies are told by only 5% of subjects') does not contain the spoken digit '1,000' (and row c04 notes N = 998). The approved row claim in claims.md was 'In a US national survey, about 60% of people said they had told no lies in the past day...'. Speaking the digit '1,000' exceeds what the row's verbatim quote supports.
blockers.fix: In a US national survey, about 60% reported no lies at all in the past day (c03).

suggestions.fix: Lying shows up around age 2 to 3 (c08).

keep.quote: You've heard it. You're lied to 10 to 200 times a day. A 2011 talk said so. It named no study (c12).
Untrained, people tell a lie from the truth about 54% of the time (c06). Everyone else is a coin flip that wants to believe you.

So the network brings in a machine. In 2003, a National Research Council report found little scientific basis for expecting a polygraph to be extremely accurate (c09), though specific-incident tests do beat chance (c09).
